title: SELLING A SERVICE
content:
You may not need to invent or source a product at all. You may already know how to do something another person or business would pay to have done.

Services can be accessible because they can often begin with skills, knowledge, tools, or experience you already have. They can be local or remote, one-off or ongoing, highly customized or standardized.

The major difference from many products is time dependence. A $30 digital product might be sold 100 times without being recreated 100 times. A $30 service usually requires some amount of fulfillment for every customer.

That does not make services worse. It simply means your time and capacity are part of the model.

SERVICES LET YOU SELL CAPABILITY
A service lets the useful thing be your ability to produce a result. That can shorten the path from idea to something sellable because you may already have the skill, knowledge, tools, or experience.

THE TRADEOFF IS FULFILLMENT
Cleaning, editing, photography, repair, bookkeeping, design, and other services require work for each customer. Some services are highly valuable precisely because that work requires skill, judgment, trust, equipment, or time.

The question is not whether a service is scalable enough. It is whether the economics and workload fit the business you want.

SERVICE EXAMPLES
One-off local: furniture assembly.
Recurring local: lawn care.
One-off remote: resume rewrite.
Recurring remote: bookkeeping.
Custom: brand strategy built around one client's situation.
Standardized: a fixed monthly reconciliation package.

All are services because the customer is paying for work to be performed. The other labels describe how that work is packaged.

Would you rather make money from something you can do for someone?

YES → PDF 40.
NO → PDF 02.

A SERVICE CAN STILL BECOME A BUSINESS
Time dependence does not mean the only outcome is buying yourself a job. A service can be priced around expertise, standardized, scheduled efficiently, delivered by a team, or later combined with products. Those are possibilities, not requirements. At this stage, the question is whether you like the core idea of getting paid to perform useful work for a customer.

WHY SERVICES ARE OFTEN AN ACCESSIBLE STARTING POINT

A product usually requires you to create, source, license, or develop something before the customer can buy it. A service can sometimes begin with a capability you already have.

That might be bookkeeping, cleaning, photography, tutoring, editing, repair, organization, design, administrative support, childcare, pet care, landscaping, consulting, or hundreds of other forms of useful work.

The fact that a skill feels ordinary to you does not make it worthless. People routinely pay for work they could theoretically learn or perform themselves because they lack the time, confidence, equipment, interest, experience, or desire to do it.

THE CENTRAL TRADEOFF IS CAPACITY

If a digital guide takes ten hours to create, selling the hundredth copy does not normally require another ten hours of writing.

If a service takes two hours to fulfill, another customer often creates more work. That relationship between customers and fulfillment time is what this branch needs you to notice.

It does not mean services cannot scale. A service can become more standardized. Prices can reflect expertise rather than only hours. Delivery can happen in groups. Systems can reduce administrative work. Employees or contractors can eventually perform some work. Expertise can later produce products.

But those are later possibilities. Start by asking whether you like the basic exchange: a customer has a problem or task, and you get paid to use your ability to help with it.

FOLLOW A SERVICE FROM PROBLEM TO PAYMENT

Suppose a small contractor is several months behind on bookkeeping.

A bookkeeper can sell a defined cleanup project. The customer provides records and access, the bookkeeper organizes and reconciles the agreed period, resolves issues within scope, delivers the completed work, and gets paid for the project. When it is finished, the transaction can end.

The same customer may then need bookkeeping every month. Now the bookkeeper can provide an ongoing service. Each month creates new transactions to categorize, accounts to reconcile, reports to prepare, or other agreed work. The recurring payment exists because new work continues to exist.

Compare that with a bookkeeping spreadsheet sold as a digital product. Once the spreadsheet is built, another customer can receive another copy without the creator personally reconciling another set of books.

WHY SERVICES CAN REACH REVENUE QUICKLY

A service often lets you sell useful capability before building a separate product asset. If you already possess the skill and necessary tools, you may be able to perform the work as soon as you have a customer and meet any applicable requirements.

That lower creation barrier is the source of the accessibility. It is also why capacity appears sooner. Ten new product sales might mean ten automated downloads. Ten new cleaning clients, photography shoots, or bookkeeping accounts create ten sets of work.

Neither outcome is inherently preferable. They are different relationships between your effort and the customer's purchase.

WHAT "LOW STARTUP COST" DOES AND DOES NOT MEAN

A service is often described as cheap to start because you may be able to sell a skill without first paying to manufacture hundreds of products.

That does not mean every service costs almost nothing.

A cleaner may need equipment and transportation. A photographer may need expensive gear and editing software. A bookkeeper may need software, training, insurance, or other professional resources. A contractor may need licenses, tools, vehicles, employees, or substantial insurance.

The useful distinction is that many services do not require you to create and finance a separate inventory of sellable units before the first customer can pay you.

Whether a particular service is inexpensive to start depends on what is required to deliver it responsibly.

THE DECISION

Choose service if you want the thing being sold to be work you perform for a customer and the relationship between your skill, time, and their result appeals to you. The next task is discovering which service you could responsibly offer.

WHERE TO GO NEXT
If selling your capability sounds promising, go to PDF 40. If not, return to PDF 02 and investigate another kind of value.
